method.visualInspection: Every listed WebP was opened individually with view_image at available original image detail. Canonical Mirza, Farah, Nazari and Demir portraits were also viewed. No conclusions were inferred only from filenames or art prompts.
method.reading: Read all 21 complete corresponding MDX lessons, including challenges, code, recall blocks, epilogues and the branch-dependent StoryConsequence in autoencoders. Read project instructions, writing rubric, story style bible, character bible and relevant scene-bible entries.
method.limits: Artwork audit, not browser QA or exercise execution. Mobile comments are judgments from image hierarchy and detail size, not measured viewport screenshots. Plot claims compare visible pixels with the explicit lesson source. A symbolic unlabeled chart is called ambiguous where its exact meaning cannot be established.
method.identity: Across these 23, the principal improvement requested earlier is present: human faces are visible and the four cast identities are recognizable. No high-severity face, age, anatomy or clothing drift was observed. The larger remaining problem is repetitive acting and source-specific visual truth.
method.continuity: Brass hardware, green scientific displays, worn consoles and established bridge/lab/engineering cues provide broad continuity. The illustrations do not establish enough shared room geometry to certify a precise architectural plan. Different camera angles are not treated as proven continuity errors.

summary.deletion: No currently used scene in this scope should be deleted. Repetitive staging should be replaced or varied within its story slot. Only superseded outputs should be removed when replacements are verified.
summary.delight: The best moments are Demir's palm-up disbelief in Transformers.js, shared Fourier enthusiasm, the prediction lean-in and the reconstruction-error exchange. Repeated Farah-pointing/Demir-chin-rest/Nazari-crossed-arms combinations make the rest feel more formal and less playful than the writing. Variation must come from each written task, not arbitrary jokes.
summary.technical: Prioritize correct spectrogram orientation/pattern, Hann broadening rather than sharpening, and ordinary amplitude versus high error in The Anomaly. Render scientific panels from real data or native components; use image generation for people, place and mood.
summary.epiloguePolicy: Add selectively where the ending introduces an irreplaceable action or relationship turn. Most endings can reuse a context image with a meaningful display/expression state; adding a second generic lesson diagram would not improve them.

assets.observed: Demir sits at the left with a hand at his chin; Nazari stands at the right, one hand on her hip and the other indicating the dark console. Their visible faces, uniforms and ages read as the canonical pair. A small route schematic and a round waveform display establish the task without swallowing them. The empty console feels like something the learner will get to bring to life.
strengths: Clear senior/junior relationship without faceless silhouettes.
Warm brass and green light make a utilitarian bridge feel inhabitable.
The large figures and single pointing gesture survive substantial downscaling.

sourceEvidence.text: Nazari signs the deployment order and writes 86,400 in the margin: one live dashboard reading every second, all day. The archive stores one row every 33 seconds, giving it 28,800 rows over eleven days. A server would need the link to the compute bay for every one of those 86,400 daily predictions. Each trip takes 180 milliseconds, which fits the time budget. Losing the link would stop predictions altogether. An outside download server is eleven light-minutes away.
Demir opens a terminal and types `npm install`. The model is going to live where the crew lives. While the package downloads, he starts a survey of the ship's consoles, oldest chair first.

assets.storyBeat: Demir thinks installation is routine; Nazari makes him measure which backend each actual crew console can run.
assets.intendedEmotion: Affectionate professional skepticism, then earned competence.
assets.observed: The seated Demir turns from three prominent benchmark bars toward Nazari, who holds her familiar multitool like a pointer. The close framing gives both faces readable reactions. The rising bars provide an immediate performance-comparison cue, and the hardware feels used rather than showroom clean. Nazari looms somewhat over him, so the scene can read as another scolding instead of a wry reality check.
strengths: Memorable practical prop and recognizable character ages.
A clear three-option comparison at image scale.
The turn of Demir's head gives the conversation a small comic interruption.

issues.fix: Use a small console/device badge beside each test and reserve exact backend names and timings for real interface text.

sourceEvidence.text: Demir runs the backend check on every bridge station before he calls it done. Five consoles report `webgl`. The sixth (the engineering panel, oldest display on the ship) comes back `wasm`: 3.0 ms per matmul, compared with 0.5 on the bridge consoles.
So the engineering chair runs that matmul six times slower than the helm. Log it. If anyone ever has to watch from that station, I want to know what they are missing and by how much.

assets.storyBeat: Demir confronts a 404 and learns how a model manifest, weight shards and cached versions reach the browser.
assets.intendedEmotion: An approachable debugging puzzle, followed by alertness about what actually shipped.

A brass-colored secured mug and his chin-resting concentration add lived-in charm. The face is visible and youthful, with the canonical short hair and ear hardware. The tight workstation is distinct from the larger group briefings.
strengths: Strong solo debugging identity.
The manifest-and-shards visual matches the loader task conceptually.
The mug gives the ship ordinary working-life warmth without hijacking the plot.

sourceEvidence.text: Farah notices that her notebook and the bridge dashboard give scores three percentage points apart for the same reading. The server received the retrained weights hours ago, but the dashboard kept loading its cached copy. Demir reused the cache key after the weights changed. For three hours and 10,800 readings, the bridge has used last week’s weights from `deep-scan-v1` in IndexedDB.
// 'indexeddb://deep-scan-v2', and nothing reads the v1 entry after that.

sourceEvidence.text: For a full hour after the 03:10 alert, the patched pipeline holds a steady tensor count and takes 3.4 ms per reading. Demir then replays the eleven-day archive to check for problems over a longer run, and known events light up amber.
At 14:31 ship-time, it flags an unlabeled reading from a quiet part of the archive: sample 7741. Farah flagged it before the network existed. Now the whole crew can see it on the bridge dashboard.
Anomaly score: 0.518. Farah routes the reading for review. The score supplies no explanation.

assets.storyBeat: The crew compares runtime choices only after checking equivalent computation; ARIA later contributes an unsolicited comparison of her own.
assets.intendedEmotion: Curious engineering comparison, then a quiet personal surprise.
assets.observed: A doorway frames Demir at a two-screen workstation and Nazari leaning into the comparison with her multitool. Each large screen has a waveform and round gauges. The waveforms visibly differ. This could represent different timing traces, so it is not proof of numerically inconsistent predictions, but the unlabeled display fails to make parity the prerequisite. The faces are legible; the familiar supervisor-and-junior staging is less distinctive than the lesson's actual ending.
strengths: Paired screens communicate comparison immediately.
The doorway and bench give useful room variation.
Canonical faces and work clothing remain recognizable.

sourceEvidence.text: Farah queues the full Sector 7-G capture for transform overnight: 64 channels, eleven days, every window of it. Before she leaves the lab she pins two time-domain plots side by side on the main display, confirmed cosmic background on the left, the stretch the crew has been arguing about for a week on the right. Demir stares until the traces blur. Sample for sample, he cannot tell them apart.
Neither can I. That is an uncomfortable thing for a signal analyst to admit, which is why tomorrow we stop looking at time.

Farah's enthusiasm and Demir's smile provide genuine warmth.

sourceEvidence.text: Four familiar peaks appear on the lab display: 5, 12, 23 and 47 Hz. Demir reaches for the log, but Farah catches his wrist and points to a fifth peak: 73.5 Hz on the half-hertz grid, magnitude 12.0. She checks the background catalog three times. Nothing explains it.

Four familiar peaks appear on the lab display: 5, 12, 23 and 47 Hz. Demir reaches for the log, but Farah catches his wrist and points to a fifth peak: 73.5 Hz on the half-hertz grid, magnitude 12.0. She checks the background catalog three times. Nothing explains it.
Overnight, she reruns the capture with a window four times longer. Its 0.125 Hz grid puts the strongest bin at 73.375 Hz, displayed as 73.4 Hz.

assets.storyBeat: Farah abandons a steady-oscillator hypothesis and asks when the suspicious tone is present; the learner constructs a time-frequency view.

Farah points into it while Demir watches with his familiar chin-rest gesture. Faces are visible and the overall image is striking, but the luminous texture reads more like repeated broadband events than an intermittent tone confined to one frequency band.
strengths: A large, distinctive analysis surface.
Good cast recognition and clear lab continuity.

issues.finding: The plotted pattern contradicts the lesson's specified axes and signal.

issues.fix: Replace the display with a computed spectrogram: a localized horizontal frequency band appearing in separated time segments, measured background around it, and real axis labels outside the raster.

sourceEvidence.text: Like a DevTools waterfall, this plot puts time on the horizontal axis. The vertical axis shows frequency. A waterfall bar shows an event’s duration. A spectrogram’s color shows a measured magnitude. A dark cell shows a low magnitude. It does not mean the measurement is missing.
The spectrogram shows bright dashes: the tone switches on and off. Farah measures gaps of roughly 73.4 seconds. She writes "~73.4 s" on the board, keeping the tilde because the timing is approximate.
No rule of mine could have produced this image. Request: store a copy of this spectrogram in my reference partition.

sourceEvidence.text: Eight more measurements are not free either. Increasing from three inputs to eleven means a bigger first weight matrix, more parameters, and a longer training run on my hardware. You are nearly quadrupling the input width on a hunch, Ensign. Write down the accuracy you expect before you spend the compute.
// Enhanced model: 11 inputs to 32 to 16 to 1 (87% accuracy)

If the nine-point gain holds across the full archive, it would mean roughly 2,600 fewer mistakes. Nazari marks the projection as provisional. The cost also depends on which mistakes disappear. Next to Demir's signed 85 she writes the actual 87 and leaves both on the board.

assets.storyBeat: Farah diagnoses spectral leakage after an expensive false lead; applying a taper must reduce distant sidelobes without pretending to sharpen the real peak.

Visible canonical faces and a warm lab maintain approachability.

sourceEvidence.text: Now the crew has two captures to compare: sample 7741 from the archive and the new live capture. Both contain the same pattern, even though each individual sensor reading stays within its usual range.

The reconstruction error is twelve times our highest normal error. There is a 73.4 Hz component that matches no known stellar phenomenon. The LSTM's forecast error is 0.041, four times its cutoff. Two detectors flagged it. The amplitude-only check stayed quiet because the amplitude is ordinary. The other individual sensor readings are within their usual ranges too, just like 7741. We need to explain why the other checks disagree.

Across the bridge, Nazari compares it with the frequency patterns used to calibrate the ship's sensors. The correlation is 0.9987. The signal from Sector 7-G follows the same ratios as the Archimedes' sensor calibration.

Nobody answers her. On the main display the two traces sit one on top of the other, ratio for ratio. The question hanging over the bridge is one no model can score. Not "what is it" anymore: is it answering us?
